summary.text: A dead zone is a low-oxygen area in an ocean or large lake, where dissolved oxygen falls to 2 mg per litre or less.
Rivers carry excess nutrients from farm and city runoff, fuelling growth whose organic material sinks and is respired, using up the oxygen.
Below 0.5 mg of oxygen per litre animals die in large numbers, and in the 1970s oceanographers began noting more and larger dead zones.

items.prompt: Oxygen in a bay starts dropping toward low levels. What do fish and other animals there typically begin to do?

options.label: Settle on the bottom and slow down
Move toward water holding more oxygen
Stay still until conditions improve
Switch to using dissolved nitrogen

items.explain: Under hypoxic conditions, aquatic life changes behaviour to reach parts of the water with higher oxygen levels.

items.prompt: Farms upstream start spreading far more chemical fertilizer. What is the likely effect where the river meets the sea?

options.label: Clearer water with fewer algae
More oxygen from all the extra growth
A bigger low-oxygen zone offshore
Saltier water along the coast

items.explain: Fertilizer in runoff is considered the major human cause of dead zones, as rivers carry the excess nutrients to the coast.

items.prompt: Extra nutrients make algae boom near a coast. Why does that end up stripping oxygen from the bottom water?

options.label: Algae soak up the bottom oxygen through their cells
The bloom blocks wind from stirring the water
Algae release a chemical that destroys oxygen
Their remains sink and are respired, using it up

items.explain: The high productivity makes organic material that sinks and is respired, and that respiration consumes the oxygen.

items.prompt: A fjord has a shallow rock ridge across its entrance. Why might its deep water run low on oxygen even with no pollution?

options.label: Water gets trapped behind the ridge for a long time
The rock ridge absorbs oxygen from the water
Fresh water from the ridge dilutes the oxygen
Cold fjord water cannot hold any oxygen

items.explain: Shallow sills at the entrance of fjords trap water inside for long periods, a natural cause of deoxygenation.

items.prompt: A coastal dead zone appears and fades on a yearly cycle. When is it typically present?

options.label: In the depths of winter
In the warm months of summer and autumn
Only during spring snowmelt
Evenly through all four seasons

items.explain: Seasonal dead zones occur every year, typically in the warm months of summer and autumn.

items.prompt: Sediments near the Mississippi's mouth record low-oxygen events from before synthetic fertilizer existed. What do those events line up with?

options.label: Periods of high river flow
Unusually cold winters
Drops in sea level
Years of drought upstream

paragraphs.heading: Water without enough oxygen
paragraphs.text: A dead zone is a patch of ocean or large lake where the water holds too little oxygen. Scientists call this condition hypoxia, and it sets in once the dissolved oxygen in the water drops to 2 mg per litre or lower. At that point, plants and animals start shifting their behaviour to reach water richer in oxygen. If the level sinks below 0.5 mg per litre, creatures die in large numbers, and the water can no longer sustain the life it held.

paragraphs.heading: Natural, but spreading
paragraphs.text: In the past, many dead zones arose naturally. Natural causes include coastal upwelling, shifts in wind, and the patterns in which water circulates. Long residence times for water, high temperatures and strong sunlight reaching down through the water also shape whether a dead zone forms and how severe it gets. Starting in the 1970s, though, oceanographers noticed dead zones becoming more frequent and larger. These cases turn up near coasts where people live, which is also where sea life is most concentrated.

paragraphs.heading: How extra nutrients steal oxygen
paragraphs.text: Dead zones can be driven by eutrophication: an overload of nutrients in the water, particularly nitrogen and phosphorus. Rivers carry these nutrients in from city and farm runoff, a problem made worse by cutting down forests. Tiny single-celled organisms such as algae and cyanobacteria use the nutrients as building blocks, and with extra supply they multiply exponentially into an algal bloom. The organic material produced sinks to the bottom, where its breakdown by respiration uses up the oxygen and brings on hypoxia.

paragraphs.heading: The human sources
paragraphs.text: People add nutrients in several ways. Chemical fertiliser washes off into runoff and groundwater, sewage is piped straight into rivers and lakes, and large heaps of animal waste leak nutrients into groundwater. Fertiliser use is considered the main human cause of dead zones worldwide, although sewage and urban land use add to the problem too. Places hit by this kind of oxygen loss include the Baltic Sea, the northern Gulf of Mexico, Chesapeake Bay and Lake Erie.

paragraphs.heading: Counting dead zones
paragraphs.text: In 2004 the UN Environment Programme counted 146 dead zones in the world's oceans, places where depleted oxygen meant marine life could not survive. Some covered only about a square kilometre, while the biggest stretched across 70,000 square kilometres. A 2008 study put the worldwide total at 405.

paragraphs.heading: Clues buried in the mud
paragraphs.text: Low-oxygen events are not only a modern story. Near the mouth of the Mississippi River, remains of organisms in layers of sediment record four hypoxic events that happened before synthetic fertiliser existed. Those layers are dominated by species that can tolerate a lack of oxygen. The timing of the events lines up with instrument records of high river flow taken at Vicksburg, Mississippi.

paragraphs.heading: Lasting, seasonal or brief
paragraphs.text: Dead zones also differ in how long they last. Permanent ones sit in deep water where oxygen rarely climbs above 2 mg per litre. Temporary ones last just hours or days, while seasonal ones come back every year, typically in the warm months of summer and autumn. How long the water takes to recover depends on how intense the eutrophication was and how much oxygen was lost.
